title: Kartarpur Sahib

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nankana Sahib, a town mapped by a childhood. Your line was where it began. This week went from the Ravidassia community to the Harmandir's day, the Akal Takht, Bangla Sahib, Sis Ganj and Nankana. Which place stayed with you? Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

A pair of hands, cracked at the knuckles, soil under the nails. A tea glass on a wall at the edge of a field. Somewhere a tractor coughs and then goes quiet. In the middle of flat farmland near the river Ravi, a white gurdwara rises out of the green, and the fields come almost up to its walls. Yesterday we stood where Guru Nanak's life began. Today, where it ended, and what he did with the years in between: he went home to the soil.
screen: `SOIL UNDER THE NAILS.` → `A WHITE GURDWARA IN THE FIELDS.` → `HOME TO THE SOIL.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Kartarpur, the Creator's town, as year one told. Tradition says Guru Nanak settled here after his long journeys, farmed his own land, gathered a community around hymns, work and a shared kitchen, and died here. Today the gurdwara stands among fields on the Pakistani side of the border, and pilgrims come through the corridor this path met on an earlier day. Second, the hymn. Guru Nanak didn't only farm. He sang about farming. In Raag Sorath, in the Granth, he turns the whole work of a farmer into a picture of the inner life, here in paraphrase: make your mind the farmer, good deeds the work, effort the water, and your body the field. Sow the Name as the seed. Let contentment be the plank that levels the soil, and humility the fence around it. Listen to how practical that is. A farmer can't skip the water or forget the fence. Neither, in the hymn, can a seeker. Third, why it matters that he farmed. The great teacher, after all those roads, could have lived on gifts. Tradition says he chose a plow. So when Sikhs speak of earning by honest work, they can point to a field and say, there, that's where he farmed. That's today's line. Fourth, the end of the story, told briefly because year one told it fully. Tradition says that when he died here, Hindus and Muslims who both loved him laid flowers on either side of him. Today there is a memorial and a grave at Kartarpur, side by side. The place where he worked the soil is where both kept him. A field, a hymn about a field, and a farmer people of two faiths wouldn't let go.
screen: `THE CREATOR'S TOWN, AMONG FIELDS.` · `MIND THE FARMER, BODY THE FIELD.` · `HE CHOSE A PLOW.` · `A MEMORIAL AND A GRAVE, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `WHERE HE FARMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the fields. Settle, and breathe. See flat green land running to the edge of sight, a river somewhere beyond it, a white gurdwara in the middle. See a man in plain clothes walking a furrow with a plow, early, before the heat. Now walk your own field for a minute: the mind as the farmer, the body as the field. What seed are you sowing today? What fence keeps it safe? Just notice. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Kartarpur Sahib. The Creator's town, where tradition says Guru Nanak farmed his own land, gathered a community, and died. Today's word.
Your line: where he farmed. Today, do one piece of real work with your hands, wash a pan, water a plant, knead some dough, and do it slowly enough to notice it. Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Gurdwara Kartarpur Sahib, across the border in Pakistan, through the Kartarpur corridor; Sikhs remember it as the place where Guru Nanak farmed, built a community and died.
